extracted_by: hand, T-0289 — the Democrat read, July 1834
note: Vol. I No. 35, the last issue of the month. THE MOST CONSEQUENTIAL CLAIM IN THE WHOLE JULY RUN IS HERE: a town ordinance directing the Surveyor to GRADUATE South Water Street to a crown on the north line of each block and to fall so that water runs into the river at every cross street. That is the shape of the town's principal street, printed. Beside it: the election notice that names the Mansion House as E. H. Haddock's, a prices current whose building-materials section is priced, an estray, and the Hennepin post-office list. The prices table is SPLIT ACROSS TWO SEGMENTER COLUMNS — its commodity names are in page 3 column 4 and its figures in column 5 — so it takes two claims, one per column, because a locator cannot cross a column.

claims.notes: THE PROFILE OF SOUTH WATER STREET, ORDERED BY THE TOWN AND PRINTED. A crown running along the NORTH line of each block — the river side is the north side here — with the street graduated so that surface water runs off into the river at each cross-street intersection. For a reconstruction that has to decide whether the town's main street is flat, crowned or cambered, and where its water goes, this is a documented answer rather than an inferred one, and it is dated to the summer before the scene. THE LINE IS CUT down its left edge by the chancery order interleaved beside it, so the verbs are supplies: 'late South- Water Btreet' at 3446 is read '[gradu]ate South Water Street' from the ordinance's own second sentence, which prints 'shall further graduate said street' whole at 3451. That is a supply from the SAME sentence pair and is the strongest kind this run offers; it is still bracketed. THE CLERK IS NEW: Isaac Harmon attests where G. W. Snow was clerk pro tem on 6 June (1834-07-02, claim c017), so the board has a standing clerk by the end of July. No merge with the Harmon of Harmon, Loomis & Co. is declared.

claims.notes: THE TOWN'S REVENUE MACHINERY, four weeks after the assessment ordinance of 6 June that the issue of 1834-07-02 printed (claim c017 there). Together the two say: the assessor lists and values every taxable property in the corporation by 1 June and returns it by the first Wednesday of July; the collector then takes the list, gives a bond of double its amount, calls PERSONALLY on every resident charged, and after ten days may seize and sell personal property on five days' notice. A town that legislates this in its first summer is a town with property worth listing, and the ordinance is the reason a tax list of 1834 should exist. Every supply here is a word cut at the left column edge and closed from the sentence it sits in; none adds a fact. The chancery order interleaved down the right of this column (lines 3459-3520's right halves) is excluded.

claims.notes: THE MANSION HOUSE IS E. H. HADDOCK'S, AND THIS IS WHERE THE MONTH SAYS SO. The Fourth of July dinner is 'on the table at the Mansion House' (1834-07-02, claim c044); a physician's residence 'is at the Mansion-house' (c046); the Board of Trustees met 'at the house of E. H. Haddock' on 6 June (c017). This notice puts the two names in one phrase — the town's annual election is held at the Mansion House, E. H. Haddock's — which makes the Mansion House the town's public room as well as its hotel. IT DOES NOT SETTLE MADDOCK'S TAVERN: the issue of 1834-07-09 places Lot No. 7 of Block 16 'one lot east of Maddock's Tavern, on Lake street' (claim c010 there), and Maddock against Haddock is one consonant. No merge is declared, and the two anchors stay separate until an issue prints both spellings in a way that decides it. THE POLLS: nine in the morning to four precisely, on Monday 11 August 1834, for trustees serving one year.

claims.notes: THE NOTICE THE PREVIOUS ISSUE COULD ONLY GUESS AT, AND BOTH GUESSES WERE RIGHT. On 1834-07-23 this advertisement ran cut down its left edge and that issue's claim c003 supplied '[three ro]oms' and '[building on Randolph] street' inside brackets while saying plainly that the second was unread. This printing carries '3 [r]ooms and a kitchen on the lower floor' and 'on Randolph-stre[et]' in the clear. So the notice offers THREE buildings: a dwelling of three rooms and a kitchen on its lower floor; a STORE on South Water Street; and a small building on Randolph Street. THE LINES ARE OUT OF ORDER in this printing — the segmenter has put 'on Randolph-street' (3592) above 'on South Water-street' (3593) and 'Also, a STORE' (3594) below both — and the normalized reading keeps the transcription's order rather than resequencing it, with the previous week's printing as the witness for the sense. The advertiser's name is 'CHAPNAN' here and 'CE ATMA' there; 'C. H. Chapman' stays bracketed on both.

claims.notes: THE PRICE OF THE TOWN'S OWN FABRIC — poplar lumber, square timber by length, shingles, brick, stone, lime and wood, as a standing section of the Democrat's weekly prices current. For a reconstruction that has to decide what a building of 1835 Chicago was made of and what was cheap, a printed materials list from the summer before is evidence of the first order, and it names POPLAR beside pine, SQUARE TIMBER priced by length, and BRICK, STONE and LIME all available in one market. THE FIGURES ARE NOT IN THIS COLUMN. The segmenter split the table down the middle: the commodity names are here in page 3 column 4 and the figures are in column 5, where they survive as a ladder of bare numbers (lines 3946-4030). A locator cannot cross a column, so the figures are claimed separately at c006 and NEITHER CLAIM ASSERTS A PRICE FOR A NAMED MATERIAL — pairing a number in one column with a word in another is precisely the join this project does not make on position alone. The list is interleaved with the Hennepin letter list, whose lines are excluded. Furs are priced immediately above: 'Muskrat skins' (3741) and 'Raccoon do' (3744).

claims.notes: A FOURTH POST OFFICE — Hennepin, on the Illinois River — and the ONLY list in the July run that prints the dead-letter rule: uncollected by 1 October and the letters go back to the Post Office Department as dead. That is what the quarterly cycle behind all four lists actually was, and it is why Chicago's list stood for three weeks and then vanished. NINE NAMES ARE MINTED and none of them is a Chicago resident; `associated_places` says Hennepin on every one. THE LIST IS INTERLEAVED WITH THE PRICES CURRENT and cut, so seven further lines are left unminted: 'Wir. L. alay' (3729), '[uncertain: Henry shiller]' (3732), '[uncertain: Jona t. tricay]' (3753), '[uncertain: Martin Thospous]' (3754), '[uncertain: Aaron Willaace s]' (3757), '[uncertain: Alley saison]' (3760) and '[uncertain: Alone Wood]' (3767). Four of the seven carry a recognizable forename and a wrecked surname; none is supplied. Thos. Galaher jr. is the Democrat's Hennepin agent — the prospectus of 1834-07-02 lists 'Thomas Hartaell' at Hennepin (claim c028 there), which is a DIFFERENT name at the same office, and no identification is made.

claims.notes: AN ESTRAY, WHICH IS ONE OF THE KINDS OF CLAIM THIS TICKET ASKS FOR BY NAME. The procedure is the whole point: a stray is taken up by a named man in a named precinct, described to the hand and the marking, APPRAISED by two named neighbours before a justice, and the appraisal published by the county clerk. That is the legal machinery a town's loose livestock ran through, and it is evidence for what an 1830s street had wandering in it. THIS ONE IS NOT IN CHICAGO — Eagle Precinct, Lasalle county — and no Chicago estray is printed in the July run, which is an absence worth recording rather than a gap to fill. THE APPRAISED VALUE IS CUT: line 3845 reads 'ollars and seventy-fivecents, by Wm.' and the number of dollars is gone. It is NOT supplied. The first appraiser's surname is gone with it. J. Cloud is the Democrat's Ottawa agent in the prospectus of 1834-07-02 and the clerk of the Lasalle Circuit Court in this issue; the two are the same written name and no merge is needed.

claims.notes: THE DRAW-BRIDGE ADDRESS, A SECOND WITNESS, AND ONE WORD DIFFERENT. This printing reads 'the oil woods' where 1834-07-16 read 'the oak woo[ds]' (claim c010 there). OAK is the reading both printings together support — an oil wood is not a thing and an oak wood outside Chicago is — so 'o[a]k' is bracketed here and the disagreement is recorded rather than smoothed. Two independent printings of the same anchor a fortnight apart is what makes the draw-bridge placement solid; the STREET is still not named in either, and none is asserted. This is the only business in the July run placed on the river crossing.

claims.notes: ONE IMPRESSION OF THE STANDING LAKE STREET LAND-AGENCY CARD. The Democrat sets this advertisement, word for word the same, in every issue from 1834-05-14 to 1834-10-01 — twenty consecutive weeks, eighteen of which set the line ‘purchased and Sold, or by commi[s]sion’ recognisably (T-1051). The card is identified by its copy and not by its display line: the same trade (‘House and Land Agent’), the same offer of building lots in the town and the School Section, the same houses to let, and the same office on Lake street opposite Dr. Temple's. The display line is lost in the interleave (line 595 reads 'Adieu,'), and 594, 597, 599 and 601 are the woven column's fragments. THE PROPRIETOR'S NAME IS NOT READ HERE and none is supplied into the quote: the record's ‘W. G. Blanchard’ stands on T-0408's reading of the two impressions whose columns are NOT Tesseract fallbacks (1834-07-16 line 5527, 1834-09-17 line 3292) and on identity.json's declared firm merge, not on this impression. THE STREET IS NOT SET HERE: the address line reads 'dest opposite Dr. Ten plis.' and the words before 'opposite' are not 'Lake st.' on the page, so the anchor is read and the street left null.
